question: Ed and Ann both have lemonade with their lunch. Ed orders the regular size. Ann gets the large lemonade, which is \(50\%\) more than the regular. After both consume \(\tfrac34\) of their drinks, Ann gives Ed a third of what she has left, and \(2\) additional ounces. When they finish their lemonades they realize that they both drank the same amount. How many ounces of lemonade did they drink together?
solution:
Call the regular drink 2 equal parts. Since the large drink is \(50\%\) larger, it contains 3 of these parts. Together the drinks contain 5 parts.

They finish all the lemonade and drink equal amounts, so each person consumes \(\tfrac52\) parts. Ed started with 2 parts and receives lemonade only from Ann. Therefore Ann must transfer
\[
\frac52-2=\frac12
\]
of a part to Ed.

After Ann consumes \(\tfrac34\) of her drink, she has \(\tfrac14\cdot3=\tfrac34\) of a part left. One-third of that remainder is
\[
\frac13\cdot\frac34=\frac14
\]
of a part. The additional 2 ounces must make up the rest of the required transfer, namely
\[
\frac12-\frac14=\frac14
\]
of a part. Thus one whole part is \(2\div\tfrac14=8\) ounces, and the combined amount is \(5\cdot8=40\) ounces.

These sizes are feasible: the drinks start at 16 and 24 ounces. Ann has 6 ounces left when she transfers \(6/3+2=4\) ounces, making each person's total consumption 20 ounces. Together they drink \(\boxed{40}\) ounces, choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).

nodes.description: Solve word problems involving multiplication of a fraction by a whole number , e.g., by using visual fraction models and equations to represent the problem. For example, if each person at a party will eat 3/8 of a pound of roast beef, and there will be 5 people at the party, how many pounds of roast beef will be needed? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie?
nodes.label: 4.NF.B.4c

nodes.description: Interpret the product (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b equal parts; equivalently, as the result of a sequence of operations a × q ÷ b. For example, use a visual fraction model to show (2/3) × 4 = 8/3, and create a story context for this equation. Do the same with (2/3) × (4/5) = 8/15. (In general, (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd.)
nodes.label: 5.NF.B.4a

nodes.description: Solve real world problems involving multiplication of fractions and mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem.
nodes.label: 5.NF.B.6

nodes.description: Interpret whole-number quotients of whole numbers , e.g., interpret 56 ÷ 8 as the number of objects in each share when 56 objects are partitioned equally into 8 shares, or as a number of shares when 56 objects are partitioned into equal shares of 8 objects each. For example, describe a context in which a number of shares or a number of groups can be expressed as 56 ÷ 8.
nodes.label: 3.OA.A.2

nodes.description: Interpret a multiplication equation as a comparison, e.g., interpret 35 = 5 × 7 as a statement that 35 is 5 times as many as 7 and 7 times as many as 5. Represent verbal statements of multiplicative comparisons as multiplication equations.
